author: Tampa Bay Times
title: USF linebacker Mac Harris lighting it up, and lighting the way - NewsBreak
text:
9 hours ago USF linebacker Mac Harris (24) runs for a 93-yard touchdown after an interception in a Sept. 20 home triumph against South Carolina State. It was the longest pick six in program history. [ LUIS SANTANA | Times ] TAMPA — The attitude adjustment occurred at night, on a rural road about a mile and a half from his Wildwood home. As he ran, Mac Harris could hear the nocturnal screeches of the crickets and critters in the darkness.
The only illumination came from the headlights of the family’s aging black Dodge Ram, though Harris also could make out his dad’s steely glare behind the wheel. MacArthur Mykel Harris III had loafed during that afternoon’s youth football practice, telling his father he just wasn’t feeling it that day. MacArthur II’s response: Maybe I don’t feel like driving you home.
So with the suburban sprawl of The Villages in the truck’s rearview and only countryside ahead, the elder Harris ordered his 8-year-old son out of the truck and told him to jog the rest of the way.
“And I think that situation taught me, like, your situation can be a lot worse. Don’t complain, and never quit anything,” recalled Harris, who turns 24 on Saturday. “Never have a quitter’s mindset. ... That’s something he preached to me from the beginning — we don’t quit. So when you sign up for something, you’re gonna finish it, and you’re gonna do your best.”
Perhaps that partially explains why Harris — co-anchor of USF’s suddenly stout defense with fellow linebacker Jhalyn Shuler — has persisted through three losing seasons, three defensive coordinators and three head coaches (including Charlie Strong, who initially recruited him) since pledging to USF a half-dozen years ago.
The other explanation: Harris now wants to be the headlight, a swarm-to-the-ball sage who illuminates a path for younger peers to follow.
It’s something he simply didn’t have at the outset of his college career as losing, lethargy and injuries mounted.
“(Not quitting) is a piece of it. And then also, just being someone who always wants to make a situation better,” said Harris, tied for the team lead in tackles with Shuler (36).
“Situationally, bringing in more and more people who I cared about on the players’ side and then getting to a point where now they’re bringing in coaches who care about you as well. So I’d say over the years, (the program) just continued to have more and more people that I was willing to fight for.”
Now in his sixth season, this beacon also has emerged as a ball hawk. Harris’ 93-yard interception return for a touchdown in USF’s 63-14 rout of South Carolina State two weekends ago was the longest pick six in program history. He also provided the ultimate season tone-setter, forcing a fumble on Boise State’s opening possession in USF’s 34-7 win against the then-No. 25 Broncos on Aug. 28.
Through four games, Harris leads the Bulls (3-1) in sacks (four), tackles for loss (4 ½), quarterback hurries (three) and forced fumbles (two).
“Everything starts defensively down the middle,” Bulls coach Alex Golesh said. “And both of those guys (Harris and Shuler) have done a really phenomenal job of not just understanding how important their role is, but understanding that, one, you’ve got everybody watching, and two, you’ve got everybody else to get lined up.
“I think the unique thing about Mac is, Mac has had to grow up a ton — physically, emotionally. He’ll be the first to tell you that he’s had to grow up and mature in every imaginable way.”
USF quarterback Byrum Brown, left, congratulates linebacker Mac Harris after his 93-yard touchdown after an interception in a Sept. 20 home win against South Carolina State. [ LUIS SANTANA | Times ] Raised in a household with six older sisters, Harris evolved into a three-star recruit at The Villages, doubling as a dual-threat quarterback and safety. Due to injuries, he was thrust into duty as a USF rookie in 2020 (24 tackles, one interception) before suffering two torn labrums — which required two surgeries — early the following season.
For the next year and a half, as Jeff Scott was fired and replaced by Golesh, Harris languished. So did any semblance of team leadership. Harris acknowledges he didn’t earn substantial playing time in 2022 (11 games, zero starts) and felt his career was nearing an end the following season.
“That 2020, 2021 and 2022 season, everybody that was here was going through a lot,” recalled Harris, who experienced four wins in that three-year span.
“So the guys who were older than me, they were going through things that I couldn’t imagine going through as an older guy. And I would say that they didn’t have the opportunity to flourish in ways that they would’ve liked to, and it blocked them from leading in ways that I believe they would’ve liked to lead.
“The relationship with coaches, the relationship between player to player, and then going on the field and also putting it on the field — I never saw everybody connect all the dots together. Again, was it their fault? No. ... But I didn’t get to see that.”
Gradually, Harris began embracing the process — a daily, detailed commitment to elite effort — preached by Golesh, and a career resuscitation ensued. In his first start in three years, a mid-October game at Connecticut in 2023, Harris totaled seven tackles and iced the game with a late fumble recovery as USF rallied from an 11-point, fourth-quarter deficit in a 24-21 triumph.
To that point, he never previously had played weakside linebacker in a game.
“They asked me if I knew (the position), and I lied and said yes,” said Harris, who would lead USF in tackles (82) the following season. “I studied my tail off the day before practice, watched a bunch of film the day before practice just so I could be prepared. Went out there and just showed flashes that I could get the job done.”
Those flashes have evolved into steady fluorescence. The kid who once jogged home in high-beam scrutiny now lights the way for others.
“Between him and (Shuler), they understand everybody’s watching,” Golesh said. “And what it’s done is, one, it’s elevated everybody else’s play, but two, it’s elevated their own play, because they know that every single bit of what they do matters. And I think when you recognize that you’re a leader, you recognize that people are watching, you tend to either crumble or it brings out the best in you.
“He’s worked himself into a guy that, if I’m an NFL team, I’m looking and there’s a lot of position flexibility there. There’s an intelligent dude that’s playing at a high, high level, maybe as good as anybody in the country right now.”
